title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Detroit, MI | Genstone
metaDescription: Detroit rehab contractor for investors: brick bungalows, two-family flats and REO homes scoped, permitted with BSEED and built on draws tied to finished work.
intro: Detroit rewards investors who know exactly what they are buying, and punishes the ones who guess. The same block can hold a brick colonial with original plaster that only needs systems and finishes, and a stripped shell where the copper, the furnace and the water heater left in the back of a pickup. Genstone Construction gives you a written number on both before you commit capital. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks at the house you are about to bid on, estimates the repair cost, tests it against your after-repair value and tells you whether the offer still works. From there you get a line-item scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, one field manager who owns the project, and vetted, licensed local contractors who work in Detroit every week. We coordinate permits with the city, track lien waivers, and post progress so you can follow the job from out of state. You pay nothing upfront, and draws release only against completed work.
housingStock:
Most of Detroit was built in a hurry between roughly the First World War and the early 1950s, when the auto plants pulled in workers faster than builders could frame houses. That boom left the city with an enormous inventory of wood-frame and brick bungalows, Dutch colonials, Tudor revivals and two-family flats, many on narrow lots with detached garages off an alley. On the west side, Grandmont-Rosedale, Bagley and Warrendale are dominated by solid brick homes from the 1920s through the 1940s. On the east side, East English Village and Morningside mix brick colonials with smaller frame houses, while Indian Village and Boston-Edison hold large early-century homes built for executives and professionals.

For a rehab, the age matters more than the style. Original wiring in the older stock is often knob-and-tube or early cloth-insulated cable, sometimes spliced into newer circuits by a previous owner. Supply lines are frequently galvanized steel, and the drain stacks are cast iron feeding a clay sewer lateral that roots have been working on for decades. Heating ranges from converted gravity furnaces to cast-iron radiator systems with boilers, and the pipe and duct wrap around them may contain asbestos. Nearly everything predates 1978, so lead-safe work practices apply to almost any job that disturbs paint.

Basements are the other constant. Most Detroit houses sit on full basements of poured concrete, concrete block or, in the oldest homes, brick or stone. Expect efflorescence, cracked block walls pushed inward by frost and saturated clay soil, and floor drains that back up in heavy storms. Brick exteriors usually need tuckpointing and chimney work rather than replacement, which is good news for the budget when it is caught early. Wood porches and their roofs, on the other hand, are frequently rotted at the posts and need rebuilding.

commonIssues.title: Scrapped plumbing and mechanicals
commonIssues.body: Vacant Detroit houses are routinely stripped of copper supply lines, brass fittings, furnaces, water heaters and sometimes the electrical service mast. When you walk a property, look at the basement first. Cut pipes hanging from the joists mean a full repipe, and a missing meter or service drop means coordinating with DTE before the electrician can energize anything. We price these items as a complete package rather than repairs, because partial replacement on a scrapped house rarely passes inspection.

commonIssues.title: Bowed block foundation walls
commonIssues.body: Concrete block basement walls in the 1920s and 1940s stock often show a horizontal crack and an inward bow where years of frost and wet clay have pushed against them. Some are stable and only need monitoring and drainage correction. Others need wall anchors, bracing or partial rebuilding. A structural engineer’s letter is often the cheapest way to settle the question, and lenders on BRRRR refinances increasingly ask for one when an appraiser notes the crack.

commonIssues.title: Clay sewer laterals and backups
commonIssues.body: Many homes still drain through original clay tile laterals to the street. Tree roots, offset joints and partial collapses are common, and the first sign is often a stained basement floor around the drain. We recommend a camera inspection before closing on any older Detroit house. If the lateral needs replacement or lining, it belongs in the scope from the start, because discovering it after drywall is up means reopening finished work.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint and lead service lines
commonIssues.body: Almost every house in the city predates the 1978 lead paint ban, and the rental ordinance requires lead clearance before a rental certificate is issued. Window friction surfaces, porch floors and painted trim are the usual failures. Separately, many homes are still served by lead water lines between the main and the meter. Detroit’s water department is replacing them over time, but you should know the line material before you plan the plumbing.

commonIssues.title: Water-damaged plaster and roofs
commonIssues.body: A roof leak in a vacant house can run for several seasons before anyone notices. By then, the plaster ceilings upstairs are sagging, the sheathing is soft and the subfloor in the bathroom is suspect. Brick bungalows hide this damage well from the street. Expect to remove more plaster than you planned once the first ceiling comes down, and budget for sheathing replacement under any roof that has visible daylight or moss.

investorMarket:
Detroit is really several markets that share a name. The established brick neighborhoods on the west side, such as Grandmont-Rosedale, the University District and Bagley, support retail flips because owner-occupant buyers know them and lenders can find solid comparable sales. Buyers there expect refinished hardwood, updated kitchens and baths, and original details like coved ceilings or leaded glass left intact.

On the east side, East English Village and Morningside follow a similar pattern at a different price point, and they draw first-time buyers using FHA financing, which makes the 203(k) route worth considering. Further from those anchors, the city has large stretches where resale comps are thin and the stronger play is a long-term hold. Investors running BRRRR or straight rental strategies tend to concentrate in areas with steady tenant demand and houses that are structurally sound but cosmetically tired.

The two-family flats scattered through Woodbridge, Southwest Detroit and the near east side are a separate opportunity. They let you house two tenants on one roof and one foundation, though the shared mechanicals need careful planning. Corktown, Woodbridge and Indian Village are pricier and heavily scrutinized by neighbors and historic commissions, so they suit investors with patience and a higher finish budget.
permits:
Building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits in Detroit are issued by the Buildings, Safety Engineering and Environmental Department, which most people call BSEED. Almost any rehab that goes beyond paint, flooring and cabinets will need at least one trade permit, and a house that was scrapped or vacant for a long time usually needs all of them. Each trade permit carries its own inspections, and final inspections must be closed before you list or rent.

Rental property adds another layer. Detroit requires rental properties to be registered and to earn a Certificate of Compliance, which involves a city inspection and a lead clearance. If your plan is to rent, building to that inspection from day one is far cheaper than fixing failures afterward.

Homes in local historic districts, including Boston-Edison, Indian Village, Woodbridge and parts of Corktown, need approval from the Historic District Commission for many exterior changes, such as windows, doors, roofing materials and porches. Plan that review into the schedule before demolition starts. Genstone’s field manager pulls permits through the local contractors, schedules inspections and keeps the paperwork in your project file.
climate: Detroit’s winters are long, cold and wet, with repeated freeze-thaw cycles that crack concrete steps, heave sidewalks and push on basement walls. A vacant house without heat is at real risk of burst pipes and split fixtures, so any purchase made between late fall and early spring should include a winterization check and, if needed, a plan to restore heat quickly. Exterior work such as masonry, roofing and concrete is best done in the warmer months, which is why many investors line up interior demolition and rough-in for winter and save the outside for spring. Summer brings heavy thunderstorms that overload the combined sewer system, and several neighborhoods have seen widespread basement flooding. Backwater valves, sump pumps where appropriate, and proper downspout drainage are worth pricing on nearly every Detroit rehab.

faqs.q: Can Genstone look at a Detroit house before I make an offer?
faqs.a: Yes. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is designed for exactly that moment. Send us the address, photos and any inspection notes you have, and we estimate the repair cost, flag the items that tend to blow up Detroit budgets, like scrapped plumbing, foundation movement and sewer lateral problems, and check whether your after-repair value supports the price you are considering. You get the information before you commit capital, not after.

faqs.q: Do you work on houses bought from the Detroit Land Bank Authority?
faqs.a: Yes. Land Bank houses often come with specific rehab requirements and a deadline to bring the property up to code and occupy it. We build the scope around those conditions so the work you pay for counts toward the compliance you need. Many Land Bank properties have been vacant for a long time, so we look closely at roofs, plumbing and heating, which are usually the largest line items.

faqs.q: How do draws work if I live outside Michigan?
faqs.a: You never pay upfront. Each draw on the schedule is tied to a defined piece of completed work, such as rough plumbing passed or drywall hung. Your field manager documents the milestone with photos and notes, and you can see progress without traveling to Detroit. Final payment comes after completion and your approval. Lien waivers are collected from the local contractors as the job moves forward.

faqs.q: Will my rehab pass the Detroit rental inspection?
faqs.a: If you tell us at the start that the house will be a rental, we scope it to the items the city inspection and lead clearance focus on, such as smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, handrails, egress, electrical safety and intact painted surfaces. That does not replace the city’s inspector, but it means the work is built with the certificate in mind rather than corrected afterward.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Detroit, MI | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip contractor in Detroit for brick bungalows and colonials: pre-offer repair estimates, buyer-ready finishes, BSEED permits and draws tied to work.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Detroit
fix-flip.intro: A profitable Detroit flip starts with the right neighborhood and the right house, and then depends on spending money where owner-occupant buyers will notice it. The brick bungalows and colonials of Grandmont-Rosedale, Bagley, the University District and East English Village sell to buyers who love original character but expect modern systems. Genstone Construction helps you price that balance before you buy. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and checks them against realistic resale comps, so you know whether the spread is there. Once you close, you get a detailed scope with finish options, a designated field manager, and licensed local contractors who handle permits through BSEED. Draws are tied to completed work, which keeps your capital moving only as the house moves toward listing.

sections.h2: Where Detroit flips find their buyers
sections.body:
Flips in Detroit work best where an owner-occupant buyer already wants to live and an appraiser can find recent sales to support your price. The west side neighborhoods with deep brick housing stock, such as Grandmont-Rosedale, Bagley and the University District, have that combination. So do East English Village and Morningside on the east side. Buyers in these areas often come from the suburbs or from other parts of the city, and many are using conventional or FHA loans, which means the appraisal and the buyer’s inspection both matter.

Outside those anchors, the resale math can change sharply from one block to the next. A beautifully finished house on a street with several vacant lots may struggle to appraise. Before you buy, we look at the comps you are relying on and compare the finish level they reflect to the scope we are pricing. If the closest comparable sales are modest, we will tell you, and we will suggest a finish level that matches the street rather than one that overshoots it.

sections.h2: Spending on what Detroit buyers notice
sections.body:
Detroit buyers are drawn to the character of the older brick homes: plaster coves, arched doorways, built-in cabinets, fireplaces with tile surrounds and oak floors. Keeping and restoring those features usually costs less than replacing them and makes the listing photos stand out. Where we see value is in refinished floors, a kitchen that opens up without losing all the original trim, a fully updated bath, and fresh paint throughout.

The less visible items matter just as much because buyer inspections in this city are thorough. Inspectors look closely at the electrical panel, the age of the furnace and water heater, the condition of the sewer line and any cracks in the basement. Showing a buyer a new panel, a camera-scoped sewer lateral and documented foundation repairs can save a deal that might otherwise fall apart during the inspection period. We put these items into the base scope so they are not discovered after the house is listed.

Every month a flip sits unfinished costs you interest, insurance, utilities and taxes. In Detroit, the most common source of delay is surprise work in a house that was vacant longer than anyone realized. Burst pipes, a collapsed sewer lateral, or a roof that leaked into the plaster can add weeks if they show up mid-project.

Our approach is to find those problems during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and the first site walk, not after demolition. The detailed scope lays out labor, materials and a draw schedule, so you can see how the project will move from rough-in to finishes. Your field manager coordinates the trades so the electrician, plumber and HVAC installer finish their rough work before inspections are scheduled, and the drywall crew is not waiting on a failed inspection. If something unexpected does turn up, you get a written change order with photos before any additional work starts.

faqs.q: Which Detroit neighborhoods do you recommend for flips?
faqs.a: We do not pick neighborhoods for you, but we can tell you how a scope looks in different areas. Houses in Grandmont-Rosedale, the University District, Bagley and East English Village tend to have stronger comps and more owner-occupant demand, so a fuller renovation usually makes sense there. In areas with thinner comps, we often recommend a lighter, durable finish and a hard look at whether a rental strategy fits better.

faqs.q: Do I need to replace original plaster in a Detroit flip?
faqs.a: Not usually. Sound plaster can be repaired and skim-coated, and buyers often prefer it to drywall in older homes. Plaster that is water-damaged, loose from the lath or opened up for rewiring and plumbing is a different story. In those areas, replacing with drywall is faster and cleaner. Your scope will mark which rooms keep plaster and which get new walls, so the finish looks consistent.

faqs.q: Can you handle the permits for my flip?
faqs.a: Yes. The licensed local contractors we coordinate pull the trade permits through BSEED, and your field manager schedules the inspections and tracks the results. Closed permits matter when you sell, because a buyer’s agent or lender may ask for them. Having everything documented in your project file makes it easier to answer those questions quickly and keep the sale on track.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Detroit, MI | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR contractor in Detroit: rehab brick homes to pass the refinance appraisal and the city rental inspection, with durable finishes and draw-based payment.
brrrr.intro: In Detroit, the BRRRR method lives or dies on two inspections that come after the construction is finished: the appraiser who sets your refinance value and the city inspector who decides whether you can legally rent the house. Genstone Construction scopes your rehab with both of those visits in mind. We start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that estimates your repair costs and tests them against the value you need for the refinance. Then we build a scope that puts money into the systems, finishes and safety items an appraiser and a rental inspector will both look at, without spending on luxury touches the rent will never repay. Licensed local contractors do the work, a designated field manager runs the project, and you pay through draws tied to completed milestones.

sections.body:
Your refinance appraisal will compare your finished house to recent sales of similar homes nearby. In Detroit, that comparison is sensitive to condition. A house with new mechanicals, a sound roof, a dry basement and a clean, updated interior is easier to support at a higher value than one that looks freshly painted but still has an old furnace and a weeping block wall.

We look at the sales your lender is likely to use and match the scope to them. In the brick neighborhoods of the west side and in East English Village, that often means refinished hardwood, an updated kitchen with durable counters, a rebuilt bath, new windows where the old ones are failing, and visible proof of mechanical upgrades. In areas where sales are thinner, we focus the budget on the items that show up in an appraisal’s condition rating and avoid finishes the comps will not support. Our scope documents every major upgrade so you can hand the appraiser a clear list.

sections.h2: Passing the Detroit rental inspection the first time
sections.body:
Detroit requires rental properties to be registered and to obtain a Certificate of Compliance, which involves an inspection and a lead clearance. For a BRRRR investor, failing that inspection delays your first rent payment and can complicate the refinance. We build the compliance items into the rehab rather than treating them as a punch list.

That includes working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in the right locations, handrails on every stair, secure guardrails on porches, egress windows where bedrooms require them, GFCI protection near water, and a safe, permitted electrical system. On the lead side, it means intact painted surfaces, especially at windows, doors, porches and stairs. Older Detroit houses almost always have lead paint somewhere, so we plan for lead-safe work practices and cleaning before clearance testing. Your field manager keeps records of what was done so you can show the inspector the work, and so the lender reviewing your refinance can see that the house is legally rentable.

sections.h2: Finishes that survive Detroit tenants and winters
sections.body:
A rental finish in Detroit has to handle tenant turnover and a long, wet winter. Luxury vinyl plank holds up well in kitchens, baths and basements, where moisture is common. Refinished hardwood can stay in living rooms and bedrooms if it is in good condition, since it tends to last longer than carpet and refinishes well at turnover.

We favor semi-gloss paint on trim and doors, solid-surface or quartz counters that do not chip easily, and simple, standard fixtures that are easy to replace. In the basement, we look at water management first: downspout extensions, grading, sump pumps or backwater valves where needed. We often recommend replacing old gravity or boiler systems with a high-efficiency furnace, because tenants will push you on heating costs and a reliable system reduces winter calls. Every choice is made with the rent you expect and the refinance value you need in mind, and with the cost of the next turnover already priced in.

faqs.q: How do I know if a Detroit house will appraise high enough to refinance?
faqs.a: We cannot set the appraisal, but we can help you test the numbers before you buy. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares the repair cost to the after-repair value you are counting on and the comparable sales near the house. If the comps do not support the refinance value your plan requires, we will tell you that before you commit to the purchase, not after the rehab.

faqs.q: Should I keep the boiler in an older Detroit house?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A working cast-iron boiler with radiators can provide comfortable heat for decades, and tenants often like it. If the boiler is old, has been frozen, or has damaged piping, replacement may be the better choice. Converting to forced air also gives you room for central air. We price both options so you can compare the upfront cost against rent and maintenance.

faqs.q: Can I use Genstone Financial for my BRRRR project?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip loans, DSCR rental loans and lines of credit, which can fit the buy-renovate-refinance cycle. You can use any lender you like with Genstone Construction. If you work with Genstone Financial, the scope, estimate and draw schedule we prepare give the loan team a clear picture of the project, which helps when the refinance comes due on a Detroit house that changed a great deal during the rehab.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Detroit, MI | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Detroit rental renovation for single-family portfolios: durable, inspection-ready rehabs and turns built for the city's rental certificate and long winters.
rental-renovation.intro: A large share of Detroit’s single-family houses are now rentals, and many of them are owned by investors who live elsewhere. Managing it well means repeatable standards, honest scopes and contractors who show up. Genstone Construction renovates and turns single-family rentals across the city, from brick bungalows in Warrendale to frame houses on the east side. We build to a consistent portfolio standard that focuses on durability, safety and the items Detroit’s rental inspection checks. Every project starts with a written scope and estimate, is run by one field manager, and is carried out by vetted, licensed local contractors. You get documentation and progress updates without having to visit, and payment is tied to completed work. Genstone Field Services can also handle inspections, occupied maintenance and turns between tenants.

sections.h2: A portfolio standard for Detroit rentals
sections.body:
Single-family rental owners in Detroit benefit from treating every house the same way. A written standard covering paint colors, flooring, fixtures, appliances, hardware and mechanical equipment makes estimates more predictable and turns faster, and it simplifies ordering. We help you set one up that fits the city’s housing stock.

For most portfolios, that means luxury vinyl plank in kitchens, baths and basements, refinished hardwood or carpet in bedrooms depending on condition, a single neutral paint color with semi-gloss trim, standard white or stainless appliances, and simple brushed nickel or black fixtures. Mechanically, it means a high-efficiency furnace, a new water heater when the old one is near the end of its life, a modern electrical panel and GFCI protection where required. Using the same products across your Detroit houses means the local contractors know the standard and your property manager can stock spare parts. It also makes it easier to compare a bungalow in Warrendale with a colonial in Morningside on cost per house.

Detroit’s rental ordinance requires registration, a city inspection and lead clearance before the Certificate of Compliance is issued. For a portfolio owner, that is not a one-time hurdle. Certificates must be renewed, and houses can fall out of compliance when tenants move out and leave damage behind.

We treat compliance as part of the scope rather than as a separate task. Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, handrails, guardrails, egress, electrical safety, working heat and intact paint are checked on every project. Window sashes and porch floors receive extra attention because they are the most common lead hazards in older houses. When we turn a unit, we look at the same items so your certificate stays current. Having consistent documentation across your Detroit houses also makes it easier to respond if the city or a tenant raises an issue. When the renewal inspection comes around, your property manager can pull the file for that address and see exactly what was installed and when.

Turnover is where rental returns are made or lost. A Detroit turn often includes paint touch-up, cleaning, flooring repair, appliance checks and fixing whatever the last tenant broke. With a defined standard, we can price turns quickly and keep vacancy time short.

Winter adds risk. A vacant rental without heat can freeze within days during a cold snap, splitting supply lines and cracking toilet tanks. If a house will be vacant during the colder months, we recommend keeping the heat on at a safe setting or fully winterizing the plumbing. Before winter, it is worth checking furnaces, cleaning gutters, extending downspouts and confirming that sump pumps work. Many of the most expensive Detroit rental repairs come from water: burst pipes, roof leaks and basement backups. Spending a little on prevention before the season changes avoids larger emergency calls later. Genstone Field Services can run those pre-winter checks across your Detroit houses on one schedule.

faqs.q: Can you renovate several Detroit rentals at once?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates a large network of licensed, insured local contractors, so we can run multiple projects in parallel. Each house still gets its own scope and its own field manager oversight, but working from a shared portfolio standard keeps pricing and finishes consistent. You can see the status of every project in one place instead of chasing several contractors yourself.

faqs.q: Do you work on occupied rentals?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services handles occupied maintenance, and our construction team can schedule larger repairs around tenants. Occupied work requires notice, clear access arrangements and attention to dust and lead-safe practices, especially in older Detroit houses. We coordinate with your property manager so tenants know when contractors will arrive and what areas will be affected, and we keep heat and water outages short in winter.

faqs.q: Is tenant damage covered by your warranty?
faqs.a: No. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers defects in the work we performed, but it does not cover tenant damage or normal wear. That is one reason we favor durable materials in rental scopes. If a tenant damages a unit, we can price the repair as a separate job and add it to your turnover schedule, with photos you can use when settling the security deposit.

multifamily-renovation.title: Two-Family Flat Renovation in Detroit, MI | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Detroit duplex and two-family flat renovation: upper/lower units, shared basements and separated utilities, phased around tenants and permitted with BSEED.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Two-Family Flat Renovation in Detroit
multifamily-renovation.intro: Detroit’s small multifamily stock is dominated by the two-family flat: one unit downstairs, one unit upstairs, often with separate front doors on a shared porch and a single basement below. You will find them in Woodbridge, Southwest Detroit, the near east side and along older streets across the city, along with a smaller number of side-by-side duplexes and converted single-family homes. Genstone Construction renovates these buildings for investors who want two rents on one lot. We plan the work around the parts that are shared, such as the roof, foundation, basement and sometimes the heating plant, and around tenants if one unit is occupied. You get a detailed scope and estimate, a field manager who coordinates the trades, and licensed local contractors who pull permits through BSEED.

sections.body:
The typical Detroit flat was built in the 1910s and 1920s for working families who wanted rental income or room for relatives. The two units usually have nearly identical floor plans, stacked one over the other, with a rear stair leading to the upper unit and a shared basement for laundry and storage. Some have separate furnaces and meters for each unit, while others still share a single boiler or electric service.

That shared design affects how you renovate. Plumbing stacks run through both units, so a leak upstairs shows up in the lower ceiling. Fire separation between the units may be weak or missing, especially if the building was altered over the years. The rear stairs and upper porches are often in poor condition and need structural work before they can be used safely. During the pre-offer review, we look for these shared issues first, because they affect both rents and usually cost more than the cosmetic updates inside each unit.

Separating utilities is one of the most valuable improvements in a Detroit flat. If both units share a boiler or meter, the owner pays for heat or power and tenants have little reason to conserve. Installing separate furnaces, water heaters and electric meters lets each tenant pay their own bills and reduces your operating costs.

The work involves more than adding equipment. Separate ductwork has to be routed for each unit, which can be difficult in buildings designed for radiators. Electrical services must be upgraded and split, and DTE has to set the new meters. Gas lines may need to be rerun. Each step requires permits and inspections. We map out the full plan, including where equipment will go in the basement and how ducts will reach the upper unit, so you understand the scope before committing. In some buildings, keeping a shared boiler and adjusting rents is the more practical choice, and we will tell you when that is the case.

sections.h2: Renovating with a tenant upstairs or down
sections.body:
Many investors buy flats with one unit occupied. Renovating the vacant unit while a tenant lives in the other requires planning. Contractors need to work during reasonable hours, keep shared areas clean, and avoid shutting off water, power or heat without notice. Lead-safe practices are especially important because dust can travel between units through shared stairways and basements.

We usually phase the work so that shared systems, such as the roof, the foundation, the main sewer line and the electrical service, are handled in short, scheduled windows with advance notice to the tenant. Interior work in the vacant unit can then continue on a normal schedule. If the occupied unit needs repairs, we can plan that for after the tenant moves out or coordinate it with your property manager. This phased approach keeps one rent coming in while the building is improved, and reduces conflict with the tenant who stays.

faqs.q: Does Detroit treat a two-family flat as a rental for inspection purposes?
faqs.a: Yes. If you rent either unit, the building falls under the city’s rental registration and Certificate of Compliance requirements, including lead clearance. Both units and the shared areas, such as stairs, porches and the basement, are part of the picture. We scope the renovation with those requirements in mind so the building is ready for inspection when the work is done.

faqs.q: Is it worth converting a flat back to a single-family home?
faqs.a: Sometimes, especially in neighborhoods where owner-occupant buyers pay more for large single-family homes than investors pay for two rents. It is a significant project involving zoning, permits, plumbing, kitchen removal and stair changes. We can price both paths, renovating as a two-unit or converting, so you can compare them against the comparable sales and rents in that area. Woodbridge and parts of the near east side are where this question comes up most.

faqs.q: What usually needs the most work in an older Detroit flat?
faqs.a: The rear stairs and upper porches, the roof, the shared basement and the plumbing stacks are the most common big-ticket items. Electrical systems often need upgrading, especially if the units still share a service. Inside each unit, kitchens and baths drive the cosmetic budget. Our pre-offer review focuses on the shared items first because they affect both units, and a failing rear stair can keep the upper unit from being rented at all.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Detroit, MI | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Detroit: bids, scopes and draw documentation for buyers, agents and lenders financing older brick homes with renovation.
fha-203k.intro: The FHA 203(k) loan lets a Detroit buyer finance the purchase of a house and the cost of renovating it in a single mortgage. That fits the city well, because so many affordable homes are structurally sound but need new mechanicals, a roof or a kitchen before they are ready to live in. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor. We work with buyers, real estate agents, loan officers and 203(k) consultants to prepare bids, detailed scopes and draw documentation that meet the program’s requirements. Our field manager runs the project from start to finish, and licensed local contractors complete the work under permits issued by BSEED. Because draws follow the program’s schedule and are tied to completed work, buyers can see exactly how their renovation money is being used.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard 203(k) for Detroit houses
sections.body:
The FHA offers two versions of the program. The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs up to $75,000, which works for a Detroit bungalow that needs a new furnace, a roof, updated electrical, a kitchen and paint. It is simpler and usually faster to close.

The Standard 203(k) is for larger or structural projects and requires a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant. It has a $5,000 minimum repair cost and is the right choice when the work includes foundation repair on a bowed block wall, removing load-bearing walls, adding a bathroom or major reconfiguration. A Standard loan also requires a consultant’s inspections during draws, with additional requirements once repairs reach the $15,000 inspection threshold. Many older Detroit homes with structural issues in the basement or roof framing will need the Standard version. We help you and your lender decide which fits by preparing a scope that clearly separates structural and non-structural work, so nobody discovers late that the loan type is wrong.

sections.h2: Which Detroit homes fit the program
sections.body:
The best 203(k) candidates in Detroit are solid houses in neighborhoods where buyers want to live, but which need more work than a conventional loan would allow. Brick bungalows and colonials in Grandmont-Rosedale, Bagley, East English Village and Morningside often fit that profile. They have good bones, but they may have outdated wiring, old furnaces, failing roofs or kitchens that have not been updated in decades.

Houses that have been vacant for a long time are harder. Scrapped plumbing, frozen boilers, damaged plaster and major roof leaks can push the scope beyond what the loan can support relative to the home’s value. Homes in historic districts like Boston-Edison or Indian Village can also work, but exterior changes may require Historic District Commission review, which adds time to the schedule. During our review, we will tell you whether the repair cost and the expected appraised value make sense together, before the buyer pays for appraisals and consultant fees.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws in Detroit
sections.body:
The 203(k) process depends on paperwork. Your lender will need a detailed bid that lists each repair, its cost and the materials to be used. For a Standard loan, that bid is reviewed against the consultant’s work write-up. Genstone prepares bids in the format lenders and consultants expect, with labor, materials and permit costs broken out by item.

Once the loan closes, repair funds sit in an escrow account and are released in draws as work is completed. For each draw, the consultant or lender inspects the work and confirms it matches the approved scope. Our field manager coordinates those inspections, provides photos and documentation, and collects lien waivers from the local contractors. We also make sure BSEED permits are pulled and inspected as required, which lenders and consultants often ask to see before releasing the final draw. Buyers are kept informed throughout, so there are no surprises about where the renovation stands.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) loan on a Detroit Land Bank home?
faqs.a: Possibly, depending on the property’s condition, the lender’s requirements and the Land Bank’s sale terms. Some Land Bank homes need too much work to fit the loan, while others are good candidates. Talk to your lender and the Land Bank about the specific property. We can provide a scope and bid to help everyone see whether the numbers work, including any rehab conditions the Land Bank attaches to the sale.

faqs.q: Do real estate agents in Detroit work with you on 203(k) deals?
faqs.a: Yes. Agents often bring us in when a buyer falls in love with a house that needs work. We can walk the property, prepare a preliminary scope and give the agent and buyer a clearer sense of whether a Limited or Standard loan fits. Having a contractor ready early helps keep the purchase timeline on track, because the lender cannot finalize the loan amount until the bid is in hand.

faqs.q: What happens if the contractor finds more damage after closing?
faqs.a: Most 203(k) loans include a contingency reserve for unexpected repairs. If hidden damage appears, such as rotted subfloor under a bathroom or a cracked drain line, we document it and submit a change order to the lender and consultant. The work proceeds once approved. We try to catch as much as possible during the initial scope to reduce surprises, including a sewer camera on older Detroit homes.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Detroit, MI | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Detroit REO and bank-owned renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: freeze damage, scrapped systems, code violations and documented, draw-based repairs.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Detroit
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned property in Detroit often reaches the asset manager after months or years of vacancy. By the time a servicer or lender takes control, the house may have been scrapped, frozen, broken into or cited by the city. Genstone Construction works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises to bring Detroit REO properties back to marketable condition. We are a preferred contractor for GSEs and understand the documentation, photo standards and approval steps asset managers rely on. Our estimators provide detailed bids, a field manager runs each project, and licensed local contractors complete the work under city permits. Genstone Field Services can also secure the property, perform inspections and handle preservation before and after the renovation.

sections.h2: What vacancy does to a Detroit house
sections.body:
A vacant Detroit house deteriorates in predictable ways. Without heat, water left in the pipes freezes during the first serious cold snap, splitting copper or galvanized lines and cracking toilets and water heaters. If the water was not shut off at the street, the resulting leak can soak floors, collapse ceilings and flood the basement. Mold grows quickly on wet plaster and wood.

Vacant houses are also targets for scrappers, who remove copper plumbing, furnaces, water heaters, aluminum siding and electrical wiring. Broken windows and doors let in weather, animals and squatters. Roofs that go unrepaired leak into the attic and walls. By the time the REO asset manager receives the file, the property may need far more than a cosmetic refresh. Our estimators look for each of these conditions and document them with photos so the asset manager can approve a scope that reflects the house’s actual condition rather than the one in the original broker price opinion.

Detroit actively cites vacant and blighted properties, and REO owners often inherit those violations. Tickets for overgrown lots, open structures, debris and unsafe conditions can follow the property, and the city may require that certain repairs be completed within a set period. Before the renovation starts, we review the property’s violation history where available and build the corrective work into the scope.

Once the renovation begins, the local contractors pull permits through BSEED for electrical, plumbing, mechanical and building work as needed. If the property will be sold to an investor who plans to rent it, the buyer will need to meet the city’s rental registration and inspection requirements. Completing permitted, documented repairs before sale makes the property more marketable and reduces the risk of the sale stalling over unresolved violations. Our field manager keeps permit and inspection records in the project file for the asset manager, ready to hand to a buyer’s agent who asks.

sections.h2: Documentation asset managers can rely on
sections.body:
Servicers and GSEs depend on detailed documentation to approve bids, release funds and defend decisions to investors and regulators. We provide before, during and after photos for each line item, written bids that break out labor, materials and debris removal, and clear notes on any conditions that change the scope. Dumpster and debris costs are included in our estimates, which matters on Detroit REO properties that often come with heavy trash-outs.

Our field managers track progress against the approved scope and submit change orders with photo support when hidden damage is found. Lien waivers are collected from contractors, and the project file stays organized so it can be audited later. Because Genstone also operates Field Services, we can coordinate preservation tasks such as securing, winterization, lawn care and inspections with the renovation itself. That gives the asset manager a single point of contact for the property from the time it is taken over until it is ready to list.

faqs.q: Can you winterize a Detroit REO property before renovation starts?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, including winterization, securing and inspections. If a property is taken over during the colder months, winterizing the plumbing quickly can prevent the freeze damage that turns a moderate repair into a large one. We can then move into the renovation when the asset manager approves the scope, and restore heat first if work will continue through a Detroit winter.

faqs.q: Do you work directly with GSEs and mortgage servicers?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises and works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs and investment funds. We follow the bid formats, photo standards and approval steps that asset managers use, and provide the documentation needed to release funds and close out projects. On Detroit files, that includes notes on city violations and permit status so the asset manager can see what is outstanding.

faqs.q: How do you handle squatters or occupied REO homes?
faqs.a: We do not remove occupants. That is a legal matter for the property owner and their counsel. Once the property is vacant and the owner authorizes access, we can secure it, assess the damage and begin the renovation. If occupants have caused damage, we document it with photos so the asset manager has a clear record, and we change locks and board openings as directed.
